Electrochemistry is a fascinating branch of chemistry, where some substances undergo interesting reactions under the influence of electricity. For example, when electrolyzing acetic acid or sodium acetate solutions in different systems, the electrolysis products will vary depending on the most easily electron-losing part of acetic acid (sodium). Now there are the following statements:

1. When electrolyzing aqueous sodium acetate solution at normal temperature and pressure, 1.5 mol of gas will be produced at the anode for every 1 mol of electrons passed.

2. When electrolyzing aqueous sodium acetate solution at normal temperature and pressure, 0.25 mol of gas will be produced at the anode for every 1 mol of electrons passed.

3. When electrolyzing acetic acid in liquid $\mathrm{HF}$ solution at normal temperature and pressure, if the main product at the anode does not contain hydrogen and the mass fraction of $\mathrm{C}$ is $22.9\%$, then 0.167 mol of acetic acid is consumed for every 1 mol of electrons passed.

4. When electrolyzing acetic acid in liquid $\mathrm{HF}$ solution at normal temperature and pressure, if the oxidation product at the anode does not contain hydrogen and the mass fraction of $\mathrm{C}$ is $22.9\%$, then 0.125 mol of acetic acid is consumed for every 1 mol of electrons passed.

5. When electrolyzing acetic acid in liquid $\mathrm{HF}$ solution at normal temperature and pressure, if the oxidation product at the anode does not contain hydrogen and the mass fraction of $\mathrm{C}$ is $22.9\%$, then under this condition, acetic acid has two or more oxidation products, including $\mathrm{CO_2}$.

Which of the above statements are correct?

For each hydrogen bond in the paired bases \( D_1/R_1/D_2/R_2 \), the atomic number of the hydrogen bond donor is denoted as \( h_n \) (\( n=1\sim 2/3 \)), and the atomic number of the hydrogen bond acceptor is denoted as \( a_n \) (\( n=1\sim 2/3 \)), where \( n \) is sorted in ascending order of \( a \times h \). For the hydrogen bond pairing in the bases \( D_{1}/R_{1} \), calculate \( x_{D_{1}/R_{1}} = (a_2 - a_1) \times (h_2 - h_1) \). For the hydrogen bond pairing in the bases \( D_{2}/R_{2} \), calculate \( y_{D_{2}/R_{2}} = (a_3 - a_1) \times (h_3 - h_2) - a_2 \times h_2 \).

Polybenzimidazole PBI is a heat-resistant polymer that was studied relatively early. It has a melting point above $400 \degree \mathrm{C}$, and its films and fibers can maintain good mechanical properties up to $300 \degree \mathrm{C}$, but degrade rapidly beyond this temperature. The monomers are aromatic tetraamines and diacids or esters:

<MultiModal>![The reaction of NC1=C(N)C=C(C2=CC(N)=C(N)C=C2)C=C1 and O=C(OC1=CC=CC=C1)C2=CC(C(OC3=CC=CC=C3)=O)=CC=C2 can produce PBI](figures/superchem_8acd9c05-66fb-4c83-a504-7517d9f5bfb3__1.png)</MultiModal>

PBI has single bonds remaining in the main chain, which are easily broken when heated at high temperatures. Therefore, all-ladder polymers (molecular structure similar to a ladder) $\mathbf{A}$ are often used in aerospace equipment. It is known that the preparation of $\mathbf{A}$ requires two monomers, and the polycondensation proceeds in two steps. The first step can occur at room temperature without dehydration, and the second step occurs with slight heating, releasing two molecules of water.

<MultiModal>![The repeating unit structure of the polymer monomer is [X1]C(C1=C([X2])C=C(C(N2C3=NC4=C2C=C(N=C([X4])N5[X3])C5=C4)=O)C3=C1)=O, $\mathbf{X_1}$ is connected to $\mathbf{X_3}$; $\mathbf{X_2}$ is connected to $\mathbf{X_4}$.](figures/superchem_8acd9c05-66fb-4c83-a504-7517d9f5bfb3__2.png)</MultiModal>

4.  The two monomers for synthesizing A have a total of 14 degrees of unsaturation.

The laboratory determines the content of titanium and iron in ilmenite containing only inert impurities using the following method:  

(1) Accurately weigh a 0.4278 g sample of ilmenite into a 30 mL porcelain crucible, add 10 g potassium pyrosulfate, and fuse at 700-750°C for decomposition. After cooling, leach the fused mass into a conical flask using 80 mL of 1:1 hydrochloric acid and 20 mL of 1:1 sulfuric acid in portions. Rinse the crucible with a small amount of hot water and transfer the washings to the same conical flask.  

(2) Add 3 g aluminum foil to the conical flask containing the leachate, and heat on an electric hotplate while slowly bubbling carbon dioxide until vigorous bubbling occurs. Cool to room temperature, add 10 mL of 400 g/L ammonium thiocyanate solution, and titrate with standard ferric ammonium sulfate solution until a blood-red color indicates the endpoint. The consumption of ferric ammonium sulfate solution is 25.49 mL.  

(3) Weigh 0.2174 g of high-purity titanium dioxide, dissolve it in acid, and treat it under the same two-step conditions described above. Titrate with standard ferric ammonium sulfate solution, consuming 26.79 mL.

The reaction of $\mathbf { A } _ { 3 } \mathbf { C } _ { 2 }$ with $\mathbf { BC }$ yields a crystal $\bf{X}$ containing $\mathbf { A }$ , $\mathbf { B }$ and $\mathbf { C }$. $\bf{X}$ belongs to the orthorhombic crystal system with unit cell parameters: $a = 8 5 0 . 3$ pm, $b =$ 1028.4pm, $c = 5 0 3 . 4 ~ \mathrm { p m }$, where the arrangement of $\mathbf { A }$ and $\mathbf { C }$ is similar to that of $\mathrm {NaCl}$. It can be regarded as two deformed hexahedrons connected coplanarly along the $a$ axis to form the unit shown in the figure below. The two hexahedrons in each unit are then infinitely extended along the $c$ axis in a coplanar manner to form an infinite chain structure; the chains are not directly connected, but form an infinite three-dimensional structure by sharing $\bf C$ atoms with the $[ \mathbf { BC } _ { 3 } ]$ unit. The $[ \mathbf { BC } _ { 3 } ]$ units in $\bf{X}$ are arranged perpendicular to the $c$ axis, the $\mathbf{B}$ center has a planar triangular configuration with two orientations, and each $[ \mathbf { BC } _ { 3 } ]$ unit has a $\mathbf { B - C}$ bond parallel to the $b$ axis. It is known that all $\bf C$ atoms in the crystal participate in the coordination of $\bf B$.

Rhodium(III) chloride trihydrate $( \mathrm{RhCl_3{\cdot}3H_2O})$ is a red solid, but its composition is relatively complex; column chromatographic separation and spectroscopic studies of its aqueous solution reveal the presence of two hexacoordinate mononuclear complex molecules, $\mathbf{A_1,A_2}$; in $\mathbf{A_1}$, the chemical environment of the same kind of atom is the same. The reaction of $\mathrm{RhCl_3\cdot 3H_2O}$ with $\mathrm{CO}$ gas flow yields $\mathbf{B}$; $\mathbf{B}$ is a dinuclear complex molecule, $\mathrm{Rh}$ is 4-coordinate, $+1$ oxidation state, and the ligands are only $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ and $\mathrm{CO}$. $\mathbf{B}$ reacts with tetramethylammonium iodide to obtain $\mathbf{C}$; $\mathbf{C}$ is a 1:1 type salt, $\mathrm{Rh}$ is in the $+1$ oxidation state, and the ligands are only $\mathrm{I^-}$ and $\mathrm{CO}$. $\mathbf{B}$ is a diamagnetic species.

Using the anion of $\mathbf{C}$ as a catalyst and iodomethane as a co-catalyst, the preparation of acetic acid can be achieved: $\mathrm{CH_3OH+CO\to CH_3COOH}$ . In the reaction, the anion of $\mathbf{C}$ undergoes an oxidative addition reaction with iodomethane to obtain $\mathbf{D}$; $\mathbf{D}$ undergoes methyl migration to obtain $\mathbf{E}$; $\mathbf{E}$ coordinates with $\mathrm{CO}$ to obtain $\mathbf{F}$; $\mathbf{F}$ undergoes reductive elimination, releasing the small molecule $\mathbf{G}$ and regenerating $\mathbf{C}$; $\mathbf{G}$ reacts with water to produce acetic acid and $\mathrm{HI}$; $\mathrm{HI}$ reacts with methanol to produce iodomethane and water.

There are the following statements:

1, Ignoring hydrogen atoms, the point groups to which $\mathbf{A_1,A_2,B}$ belong are $C_{2v},C_{3v},D_{2h}$, respectively.

2, The theoretical magnetic moments of $\mathbf{A_1,C}$ are 0 and 2.83 B.M., respectively.

3, The oxidation states of $\mathrm{Rh}$ in $\mathbf{D,E,F}$ are not all the same.

4, The molecular weight of $\mathbf{G}$ is 297.9.

Then the option that contains all the correct statements is:

stem:
Chromatography is a good method for separating and identifying compounds. In chromatography, substances with different properties can be separated by the different partition ratios of compounds in the stationary phase/mobile phase. A very important value for judging the separation efficiency of chromatography is the $Rf$ value (retardation factor), which is the ratio of the distance of the separated substance to the origin to the distance of the solvent front to the origin. In addition to changing the developing solvent, there is also a common technique in the laboratory to separate two compounds on a thin-layer chromatography plate to clarify the composition of the system: after performing one $TLC$ separation, the solvent is evaporated, and then another development is performed (assuming the solvent front reaches the same height). It is known that there are two compounds in the system, and their Rf values in the developing solvent are $a$ and $b$ respectively ($0<a<b<1$).
The following statements are correct:
1. To achieve better separation with secondary development, it is required that $a<b<0.5$
2. If a=0.3, b=0.6, the separation effect of secondary development is better than that of single development.
3. If a=0.3, b=0.4, the separation effect of tertiary development is better than that of secondary development.
4. If a=0.2, b=0.3, the separation effect of tertiary development is better than that of secondary development.
5. Tertiary separation is better than secondary separation, requiring $a+b<0.67$
6. Tertiary development achieves better separation requires: $a^2+b^2+ab-3a-3b+1>0$

The following statement that is correct is:

2.  In the cation, there are two kinds of environments for $\rm Cu$ (ratio is 1:1), one of which $\rm Cu$ is connected to 6 $\rm Cu$, and the other is connected to 3 $\rm Cu$. Then $\rm Cu$ constitutes a tetracapped tetrahedron.

Teacher Hui Hui obtained a white powder $\mathbf{A}$ in the laboratory one day. $\mathbf{A}$ is a binary compound containing the non-metallic element $\mathbf{X}$, which can quantitatively absorb carbon monoxide from the air and produce another gas present in the air along with the elemental form of $\mathbf{X}$. After dissolving $\mathbf{A}$ in cold water, an excess of sodium hydroxide solution was added to obtain a certain solution. When an excess of chlorine gas was passed through this solution, a colorless solution of $\mathbf{B}$ was obtained (Reaction 1), with excess sodium hypochlorite remaining in the solution. A pale pink hydrated crystal $\mathbf{C}$ (containing the metallic element $\mathbf{Y}$) was mixed with the aforementioned colorless solution. After thorough reaction, a bright red solution was obtained, and upon adding anhydrous ethanol, a hydrated crystal $\mathbf{D}$ precipitated. $\mathbf{D}$ contains no sulfur or chlorine elements.

To verify $\mathbf{D}$ (assuming it is a pure chemical composition), Teacher Hui conducted the following validation experiments:

1) A 0.5000 g sample of $\mathbf{D}$ was heated at 150°C until constant weight was achieved, leaving a residue of 0.3664 g.

2) Excess SO₂ gas was passed through a solution containing 0.5000 g of $\mathbf{D}$ (Reaction 2). After thorough reaction, the excess SO₂ was removed by heating, and the resulting solution was divided into two portions. To the first portion, a slight excess of silver nitrate solution was added, yielding 0.1452 g of a yellow precipitate $\mathbf{E}$. After centrifuging to remove $\mathbf{E}$, a slight excess of barium nitrate solution was added to the filtrate. The resulting precipitate was washed, dried, and weighed to yield 0.6252 g of a white precipitate $\mathbf{F}$. The second portion of the solution was thoroughly cooled, and a slight excess of $NH_4HS$ solution was added, producing a pink precipitate $\mathbf{G}$ containing the element $\mathbf{Y}$. $\mathbf{G}$ is a binary compound. After drying at $100\degree\mathrm{C}$ under a nitrogen atmosphere, the weight of $\mathbf{G}$ was measured as 0.0179 g.

Additional information:

1) The metallic element $\mathbf{Y}$ commonly occurs in nature as a binary compound $\mathbf{H}$, in which the mass fraction of $\mathbf{Y}$ is 63.2%.

2) The aqueous solution of $\mathbf{C}$ can react with barium chloride solution to also produce the white precipitate $\mathbf{F}$.

3) The mass fraction of element $\mathbf{X}$ in $\mathbf{B}$ is 43.18%, and the mass fraction of element $\mathbf{Y}$ in $\mathbf{C}$ is 19.84%.

Please deduce what $\mathbf{A, B, C, E, F, G, H, X, Y}$ are. Based on the answers, first calculate and deduce the chemical formula of $\mathbf{D}$, then deduce the chemical equations for Reactions 1 and 2 (not ionic equations). Select the appropriate options based on the results.

stem:
$\mathbf{X}$ is a common $\mathbf{M}$-containing compound, which can be obtained by treating an anhydrous ether solution of $\mathbf{M}\mathrm{Cl_3}$ with hydrogen sulfide at low temperature (reaction $\mathbf{1}$). $\mathbf{X}$ is readily soluble in potassium cyanide solution, and the products contain two different sulfur-containing anions (reaction $\mathbf{2}$).  

$\mathbf{Y}$ is a neutral complex containing low-valent $\mathbf{M}$. Refluxing $\mathbf{Z}$ (containing $\mathbf{M}\ 68\ \%$), $\mathrm{Zn(NO_3)_2·6H_2O}$, and $\mathbf{L}$ in anhydrous acetonitrile solvent for 5 min, followed by crystallization of the resulting solution under an inert atmosphere, yields the complex $\mathbf{Y}$ (reaction $\mathbf{3}$). The structure of $\mathbf{L}$ is known as:  

<MultiModal>![C1=CC(=NC=C1)C2=NC=CC=C2, i.e., the structure of [L]](figures/superchem_9b5d1d4e-33ae-4a3b-b6e3-2bccb9a96372__1.png)</MultiModal>  

In $\mathbf{Y}$, both $\mathrm{Zn}$ and $\mathbf{M}$ exhibit only one coordination number, and no mirror plane is present. Elemental analysis of $\mathbf{Y}$ yields: $\mathrm{N}\ 12.8; \mathrm{C}\ 32.9; \mathrm{Zn}\ 7.46$ (all in mass fraction, $\%$).  

Which of the following statements are correct?  
1. Reaction $\mathbf{1}$ is a redox reaction, and the oxidation state of $\mathbf{M}$ remains unchanged in reaction $\mathbf{2}$.  
2. In the simplest balanced equation for reaction $\mathbf{1}$, the sum of all coefficients on the reactant side and the product side is 14.  
3. In reaction $\mathbf{2}$, the mass fraction ratio of sulfur in the two anions is 1: 0.55.  
4. In the simplest balanced equation for reaction $\mathbf{2}$, the sum of all coefficients on the reactant side and the product side is 12.  
5. In the simplest balanced equation for reaction $\mathbf{3}$, the sum of all coefficients on the reactant side and the product side is 13.  
6. $\mathbf{Y}$ is chiral.  
7. $\mathbf{Y}$ has a total of 4 reasonable stereoisomers.

stem:
In 1995, Professor Kim's research group reported the following reaction:

<MultiModal>![N1(CC1C2=CC=CC=C2)/N=C/C3C(C4=CC=CC=C4)O3 yields C#CC(C1=CC=CC=C1)O under heating conditions](figures/superchem_9b8ddb55-81c4-4cac-87d0-20baf43ef692__1.jpg)</MultiModal>

Mechanistic studies have shown that, under heating conditions, the substrate molecule first decomposes to give $\bf{A}$ and $\bf{B}$, the molecular weight of $\bf{A}$ is approximately 104, $\bf{B}$ undergoes ring-opening to give $\bf{C}$, $\bf{C}$ undergoes intramolecular proton transfer to give $\bf{D}$, $\bf{D}$ then releases a molecule of gas to give $\bf{E}$, and $\bf{E}$ undergoes a 1,2-H shift to give the product.

The following statements are made:

1. The degree of unsaturation of $\bf{A}$ is 5

2. $\bf{B}$ is a 1,3-dipole

3. $\bf{C}$ has a charge-separated structure and the types of atoms bearing the positive and negative formal charges are different

4. The gas released by $\bf{D}$ is not a common gas in the atmosphere

5. All atoms in $\bf{E}$ (except hydrogen atoms) satisfy the octet rule

Which of the following options contains the most correct statements?

Tandem mass spectrometry is a rapid method for peptide sequencing. This technique involves the formation of precursor ions and their fragmentation into smaller ions. In peptides, fragmentation often occurs on the peptide backbone. The naming of fragment ions depends on the site of fragmentation and which atom carries the positive charge. For example, some ions formed from alanyl-leucyl-glycine are shown below:

Dissolve $\rm MnCl_2\cdot 4H_2O$ in ethanol, and add an aqueous solution of $\rm Htopca$ (a carboxylic acid derivative with the molecular formula $\rm C_5H_6N_2O_3$). After mixing and stirring at 80 ℃ for 2 h, filter. The filtrate is slowly evaporated at room temperature, and a yellow blocky crystal precipitates from the solution. Thermogravimetric analysis of $\bf X$ under a nitrogen atmosphere shows that $\bf X$ loses a% of its weight between 65 and 120 ℃, corresponding to the loss of all crystal water and structural water; continue heating to 250 ℃, the weight loss is b%; continue heating to 850 ℃, the weight loss is further 14.04%, and the subsequent solid mass no longer changes. Chemical analysis of the residual solid shows that the solid contains two substances, and the mass fraction of $\rm Mn$ in the mixture is 46.17%. The mixed gas released during the second weight loss is analyzed, and the mixed gas contains three gas molecules, of which only propyne contains carbon. After cooling the mixed gas, it is fully absorbed by bromine water. The mass of the remaining gas is 37.94% of the original gas mass, and the remaining gas changes from colorless to reddish-brown in the air. It is known that $\bf X$ is a mononuclear $\rm Mn$ complex, and the oxidation state of $\rm Mn$ does not change during the thermogravimetric analysis.

Given a+b=58.07, which of the following statements are correct:
1. The sum of the number of all atoms in the chemical formula of $\bf X$ is less than 45
2. The three gases produced by the second weight loss are in a ratio of 1:1:2
3. In the total reaction equation for the second and third steps of weight loss, the sum of the coefficients on the right side is less than 12
4. The final product of the weight loss can react with concentrated sulfuric acid, producing only one gas

A laboratory attempted to synthesize compound **A** by reacting excess Vilsmeier salt with an equivalent amount of base and o-aminobenzamide, but found that no **A** was formed. Instead, a yellow, low-melting-point, non-crystalline compound **B** was obtained. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis revealed that the molecular weight of **B** was 216.28.

The laboratory then heated compound **B** with a large excess of hydroxylamine hydrochloride and an equivalent amount of sodium acetate in a methanol-water solution, intending to prepare the seven-membered cyclic compound **C** with a molecular weight of 204.23. However, thin-layer chromatography (TLC) development using dichloromethane and petroleum ether containing triethylamine revealed a non-fluorescent compound **D** and a fluorescent compound. LC-MS and <sup>1</sup>H NMR analysis confirmed that the fluorescent compound was **A**. LC-MS analysis showed that the molecular weight of **D** was also 204.23.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) confirmed that compound **D** possesses a hexa-hexacyclic system, which was not the intended structure of **C**. To investigate the reaction mechanism, diethylhydroxylamine was used instead of hydroxylamine hydrochloride and sodium acetate, but no analogs of **D** were formed.

The following options each contain three structural images: the first is the possible structure of **A**, the second is the possible structure of **C**, and the third is the possible structure of **D**. Select the option where all three structures are correct.

stem:
The boronate ester phase is attacked by the nucleophilic carbon atom of the leaving group, followed by a 1,2-migration to transform into a carbaboronate ester. This reaction is known as the Matteson reaction, which is essentially similar to the hydroboration-oxidation reaction. The research group of Guangbin Dong at the University of Chicago extended this reaction to aminoboronate esters, achieving the aza-Matteson reaction between N-B bonds. However, unlike the Matteson reaction, depending on the halogens on dihalomethane, they were able to control the formation of mono-insertion and double-insertion products.

<MultiModal>![[R]N(C1=CC=CC=C1)B2OC(C)(C)C(C)(C)O2 reacts with n-butyllithium and $CH_2XY$ at -78°C, followed by warming to room temperature and reaction with a Lewis acid.](figures/superchem_9f5f9c12-a1e9-4d2b-aaf0-a68d4d9e0448__1.png)</MultiModal>

Which of the following statements are correct?
1. When using chlorobromomethane, a double-insertion reaction can occur.
2. When using dibromomethane, a double-insertion reaction can occur.
3. The reason double insertion can occur is that nitrogen's 1,2-migration can involve lone pair electrons, making the rate faster.
4. The reason the reaction stops at the double-insertion product is that the lone pair electrons of nitrogen in the double-insertion product can coordinate with the boronate ester, preventing further reaction.

Reacting a $D_{4d}$ point group carbonyl compound $\bf{X}$ of $Mn$ with $Na$ yields a 1:1 ionic compound $\bf{A}$. $\bf{A}$ reacts with allyl chloride to produce $\bf{B}$. Heating $\bf{B}$ results in the loss of one molecule of a toxic gas, yielding $\bf{C}$. Simultaneously, $\bf{B}$ reacts with perchloric acid to produce an ionic compound $\bf{D}$. $\bf{A}$ can react with 1,3-dibromopropane to produce a neutral complex $\bf{E}$, and it can also react with $BrCH_{2}CH_{2}SMe$ to produce $\bf{F}$ (hint: one molecule of a toxic gas is also generated). $\bf{A}$ reacts with phosphoric acid to produce a mononuclear complex $ G $ with a four-fold axis. $ G $ further transforms into a trinuclear complex $\bf{H}$. $\bf{G}$ can react with diazomethane in a 1:1 ratio to produce $\bf{I}$. $\bf{X}$ can react with dimethylamine to produce a 1:2 ionic compound $\bf{J}$, while also generating a common solvent $K$. The mass fraction of the Mn element in $\bf{J}$ is $2 3 . 0 4 \%$ , and $\bf{J}$ and $\bf{A}$ have the same anion.

The following statements are made about $\bf{A}$-$K$:

1.  Both $\bf{A}$ and $\bf{B}$ satisfy the EAN rule.

2.  $\bf{C}$ does not satisfy the EAN rule.

3.  The cation in $\bf{D}$ has a $C_4$ axis.

4.  The molar mass of $\bf{E}$ is approximately 317 g/mol.

5.  $\bf{G}$ and $\bf{I}$ have the same highest order of rotational axis.

6.  $\bf{H}$ belongs to the $D_{3h}$ point group.

7.  If carbon and hydrogen atoms are ignored, the cation of $\bf{J}$ belongs to the $O_h$ point group.

Let the sum of the numbers of the correct statements be a, and the smallest number of the correct statements be b, then a and b are respectively:

The powder is recrystallized with an acetone-water mixed solvent, yielding orange-red crystals **A**. The following characterization results are obtained for **A**:

3. **A** contains neither acetone nor ethanol molecules.

stem:
Oxalate is a good ligand and can form complexes with transition metals. Since oxalate solutions are strongly alkaline, metal ions that are prone to hydrolysis, such as $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}, Al^{3+}}$, need to be converted to hydroxides first, then dissolved in oxalic acid, and neutralized with a base to obtain the corresponding oxalate complexes. This lengthy procedure is time-consuming, it is difficult to filter the hydroxides, the operation results in a lot of loss, and the yield is often not ideal.

Someone proposed the following experimental scheme to directly prepare the complex of oxalate with ferric iron: mixing $\mathrm{20 ~mL\ 3 ~mol\cdot L^{-1}}$ potassium oxalate hot solution and $\mathrm{8 ~mL\ 1.5 ~mol\cdot L^{-1}}$ ferric chloride solution, cooling to room temperature to obtain green needle-shaped crystals $\mathrm{K_3Fe(C_2O_4)_3 \cdot 3H_2O}$, and measuring the volume of the solution at this time as $\mathrm{30~mL}$. Now we theoretically calculate the feasibility of this scheme.

Constants involved in this problem: $\mathrm{pK_{sp}(Fe(OH)_{3})=38.55, \lg K_{f}(Fe(C_2O_4)_3^{3-})=20.2, pK_{b1}(C_2O_4^{2-})=9.73}$. The saturated solubility of the product at room temperature is $\mathrm{4.9~g \cdot 100 ~mL^{-1}}$, and the solubility of the two reactants is very high.

The secondary hydrolysis of oxalate is ignored in the calculation of this problem.

Which of the following options regarding this experimental scheme is correct (calculation error within 1% is considered correct):

We denote the position of the amino acid residue at the $C$-terminus of a peptide chain cleaved by a protease as 0, and sequentially forward as -1, -2, -3, and backward as +1, +2, +3, and so on. For example, the substrate recognized by trypsin is a residue at position 0 that is lysine or arginine, and the residue at position +1 is not proline.

Subtilisin is a serine/threonine protease. Subtilisin has the ability to recognize longer substrate series and has certain selectivity for different residues at positions -3 to 0. We denote the substrate pocket recognizing the 0 residue as S1, the pocket for the -1 residue as S2, -2 as S3, and -3 as S4.

In wild-type subtilisin, the S4 pocket residue is Tyr104, the S2 pocket is Asn62, and the S1 pocket is Gly166. Scientists tested the selectivity of wild-type subtilisin for different substrates using a C-terminally substituted tetrapeptide substrate XXXX-p-nitroanilide, and found that the fastest reacting sequence was Ala-Ala-Pro-Phe-p-nitroanilide.

Now we consider a batch of subtilisin mutants:

A. G166D, N62D

B. G166L, Y104D

C. N62V, Y104K

And some substrates:

1. AAPF-p-nitroanilide
2. AAPA-p-nitroanilide
3. AAPQ-p-nitroanilide
4. AAPY-p-nitroanilide
5. DAKF-p-nitroanilide
6. RAKR-p-nitroanilide
7. RGKE-p-nitroanilide
8. DAPR-p-nitroanilide
9. DAVF-p-nitroanilide
10. FGKR-p-nitroanilide
11. LGFR-p-nitroanilide
12. AAKR-p-nitroanilide
13. RGAA-p-nitroanilide
14. DAHF-p-nitroanilide
15. RGAG-p-nitroanilide

Then, matching these mutants with the substrates with which they react fastest, which of the following options has the numbers from front to back representing the substrate numbers corresponding to subtilisin A, B, and C, respectively, with completely correct results?

Calcium carbide reacts with $\mathrm{N}_{2}$ at high temperatures to yield compound $\mathbf{A}$. Hydrolysis of $\mathbf{A}$ produces an important pesticide intermediate $\mathbf{B}$. Under alkaline conditions, $\mathbf{B}$ polymerizes to form dimer $\mathbf{C}$. Heating $\mathbf{C}$ with dimethylamine hydrochloride and recrystallization yields $\mathbf{D}$. Reaction of $\mathbf{B}$ with sodium cyanide and chlorine under alkaline conditions gives the sodium salt $\mathbf{E}$. Researchers reacted $0.15\space\mathrm{g}\space\mathrm{Cu(NO_{3})_{2}{\cdot}6H_{2}O}$, $1.07\space\mathrm{g}\space \mathbf{E}$, and $0.52\space\mathrm{g}$ N,N-dimethylethylenediamine in an aqueous solution to obtain a dinuclear copper complex $\mathbf{F}$, with an experimentally determined copper mass fraction of $22.55\%$. X-ray diffraction data reveal that ligand $\mathbf{E}$ in $\mathbf{F}$ exhibits two distinct configurations—monodentate coordination and bridging coordination—in a 1:1 ratio, with both configurations utilizing the same coordinating atom.  

In the molecular structure of $\mathbf{F}$, how many bonds separate the two farthest N atoms along the shortest path?

stem:
Add $0.5~\mathrm{mmol}$ $\mathrm{Ce(NO_3)_3\cdot6H_2O}$, $0.5~\mathrm{mmol}$ $\mathrm{Fe(NO_3)_3\cdot9H_2O}$, $1~\mathrm{mmol}$ tiron, $1~\mathrm{mmol}$ phen, $2~\mathrm{mmol}$ $\mathrm{NaOH}$, $5~\mathrm{mL}$ ethanol, and $8~\mathrm{mL}$ distilled water into an $18~\mathrm{mL}$ stainless steel autoclave with a Teflon liner. React at $175~\degree\mathrm{C}$ for $4~$days, then allow to cool naturally to room temperature to obtain black-brown block-shaped single crystals with a yield of approximately $75\%$.

The molecular formula of the tiron ligand is $\mathrm{C_6H_2O_8S_2^{4-}}$, and the molecular formula of the phen ligand is $\mathrm{C_{12}H_8N_2}$. Elemental analysis of the product yielded mass fractions (%) of: $\mathrm{C}$ $47.09$; $\mathrm{N}$ $7.32$; $\mathrm{S}$ $8.38$; $\mathrm{O}$ $20.91$. Thermogravimetric analysis of the obtained crystals showed a weight loss of $4.71\%$ at $122~\degree\mathrm{C}$, corresponding to the loss of all crystalline water. The relative atomic mass of $\mathrm{Ce}$ is known to be $140.1$.

The structure of tiron is:

<MultiModal>![[O-]C1=C(S(=O)([O-])=O)C=C(S(=O)([O-])=O)C=C1[O-]](figures/superchem_b0e74a86-4843-4a47-8d2a-9124851df85c__1.png)</MultiModal>

The structure of phen is:

<MultiModal>![C12=C(N=CC=C3)C3=CC=C1C=CC=N2](figures/superchem_b0e74a86-4843-4a47-8d2a-9124851df85c__2.png)</MultiModal>

The molar conductivity of the complex measured in DMSO solvent is $139~\mathrm{S\cdot cm^2\cdot mol^{-1}}$, indicating that it is a 2:1 type electrolyte. The number of crystalline water molecules in the complex is a positive integer. The anion has a $C_3$ symmetry axis.  

The following statements are correct:  

1. The molecular formula contains $4$ crystalline water molecules.  

2. The molecular formula contains $6$ crystalline water molecules.  

3. The $\mathrm{Ce:Fe}$ ratio in the anion is $1:2$.  

4. The cation has only one stereochemical configuration.  

5. Both sulfonate groups in the anion participate in coordination.  

6. The anion has three mirror planes along the principal axis.

Chromium is a steel-gray metal extracted from red Siberian ore by the French scientist Vauquelin in 1797. It is often used in the manufacture of stainless steel and for chrome plating metal surfaces of instruments. Industrially, the preparation of elemental chromium starts from chromite ($\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4}$), which is strongly heated in air with a mixture of sodium carbonate, where iron is converted to ferric oxide (Reaction 1). The resulting solid residue is leached with water, acidified, and a chromium-containing sodium salt precipitates. This salt is then reduced to chromium oxide by heating with carbon at high temperature, simultaneously generating a salt and releasing a gas (Reaction 2). Finally, treatment with ignited metallic aluminum yields relatively pure chromium (Reaction 3).

For the extraction of molybdenum, which is in the same group as chromium, molybdenite is usually used as the raw material, which is roasted in oxygen (Reaction 4). The resulting product is leached with ammonia water to transfer molybdenum to the solution; alternatively, molybdenite can react with caustic soda solution in an oxygen atmosphere to transfer molybdenum to the solution (Reaction 5), during which sulfur is also oxidized and enters the solution. Subsequently, the ammonia-leached solution is acidified to precipitate a polyoxometalate which anion contains seven molybdenum atoms (Reaction 6, ionic equation), which is then calcined and reduced with hydrogen to obtain relatively pure metallic molybdenum.

Diverse novel species containing peroxo bonds are prepared using different methods.

Compound $\bf A$ can be prepared by bubbling $\rm CO_2$ into a concentrated aqueous hydrogen peroxide solution containing $\rm KOH$, crystallizing, while controlling the temperature at $-5\degree\rm C$ to $-20\degree\rm C$.

Compound $\bf B$ can be prepared by adding potassium bicarbonate to saturation in a $30\%$ aqueous hydrogen peroxide solution, then adding a certain amount of ethanol, and cooling to crystallize, while controlling the temperature at $-10\degree\rm C$ to $-15\degree\rm C$.

Crystal structure determination and thermal analysis indicate that:
In the crystal of $\bf A$, there is only one type of anion;

In the crystal of $\bf B$, there is only one type of cation, one type of anion, and one type of neutral molecule.

$\bf A$ loses $30.3\%$ of its weight when heated above $160\degree \rm C$ (Reaction 1);

$\bf B$ loses $53.9\%$ of its weight when heated above $200\degree\rm C$ (Reaction 2).

The following statements are made:
1. The anion structure of $\bf A$ contains a mirror plane.

2. The ratio of the number of cations, anions, and neutral molecules in the composition of $\bf B$ is $1:1:1$.

3. The solid products of the thermogravimetric analysis of $\bf A,B$ are consistent.

4. The coefficient of $\rm H_2O$ in the equation of Reaction 2 (with coprime integer coefficients) is 3. (If there is no $\rm H_2O$ in the reaction equation, this statement is considered correct)

5. Arranging $\bf A \rm,K_2O_2,O_2F_2$ according to the length of the peroxo bond, the order is $\rm K_2O_2>O_2F_2>\bf A$.

What is the sum of the serial numbers of the correct statements?

It is known that this reaction proceeds quantitatively and yields the following products (unbalanced):

$ Py + \mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{P} + ^iPrOH + CH_3COCH_3$

The structures of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ are as follows:

$\mathbf{A}$:

<MultiModal>![O=[V]12(OC(C)C)[N]3=C(C(O2)=O)C=CC=C3C(O1)=O
](figures/superchem_b406b145-3925-4ce4-9ddc-18a94b39295f__1.png)</MultiModal>

$\mathbf{P}$:

<MultiModal>![O=C(O1)C2=CC=CC(C(O3)=O)=[N]2[V]13(C4=NC=CC=C4)(C5=NC=CC=C5)OC(C)C
](figures/superchem_b406b145-3925-4ce4-9ddc-18a94b39295f__2.png)</MultiModal>

The experimental team proposed three possible reaction pathways for the pyrolysis:

$\mathbf{Path I}$

$Py + \mathbf{A} \xrightleftharpoons[]{K_{eq}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[]{k_1} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[]{fast} \mathbf{P}$

$\mathbf{Path II}$

$Py + \mathbf{A} \xrightleftharpoons[]{K_{eq}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[Py]{k_1} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[]{fast} \mathbf{P}$

$\mathbf{Path III}$

Both $ Py + \mathbf{A} \xrightleftharpoons[]{K_{eq}} \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[Py]{k_1} \mathbf{C} \xrightarrow[]{fast} \mathbf{P}$

And $ \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow[Py]{k_2} \mathbf{D} \xrightarrow[]{fast} \mathbf{P}$

The structures of $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, and $\mathbf{D}$ are as follows:

$\mathbf{B}$:

<MultiModal>![O=[V]12(OC(C)C)(C3=NC=CC=C3)[N]4=C(C(O2)=O)C=CC=C4C(O1)=O

$\mathbf{D}$:

](figures/superchem_b406b145-3925-4ce4-9ddc-18a94b39295f__5.png)</MultiModal>

It is known that in $Path II$ and $Path III$, one molecule of $py-d_5$ participates in the proton transfer process during the formation of $\mathbf{C}$ or $\mathbf{D}$, while $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are highly reactive, so their concentrations can be neglected.

Experimental measurements at $340K$ show the following variation curve of $k_{obs}$ with $[py]$:

<MultiModal>![This image is a scatter plot of the apparent rate constant $k_{obs}$ versus the concentration of perdeuterated pyridine $[pyridine]$. The x-axis represents $[pyridine]$ in units of $M$, with a range of $0-15$, and the y-axis represents $k_{obs}$ in units of $10^{-4}s$, with a range of $0-6$. The estimated coordinates of the data points are $(0,0), (0.33,0.59), (0.49,0.75), (0.98,1.47), (2.95,1.98), (5.93,2.98), (8.93,4.07), (12.40,4.96)$.](figures/superchem_b406b145-3925-4ce4-9ddc-18a94b39295f__6.png)</MultiModal>

1. For all three reaction pathways, the reaction order with respect to $[\mathbf{A}]$ is 1.

3. When $[py] \gg 1/K_{eq}$, the variation of $k_{obs}$ with $[py]$ at $340K$ best fits $\mathbf{Path I}$.

The purple double salt crystal $\mathbf{A}$ dissolves in water to form a yellow solution. Adding a colorless weakly acidic solution (solute is $\mathbf{B}$) to the solution of $\mathbf{A}$ causes the color to fade to colorless, producing $\mathbf{C}$. $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{A}$ contain the same cation, and the point group of the anion of $\mathbf{B}$ is $D_{\infty h}$. Adjusting the solution of $\mathbf{A}$ to alkaline, adding excess sodium hypochlorite for oxidation, and then reacting with $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$ produces $\mathbf{D}$, which is also purple. Adding an alkaline solution of sodium tetraphenylborate to the solution of $\mathbf{B}$ produces a white precipitate $\mathbf{E}$. The molecular weight of $\mathbf{A}$ rounded down is 503. $\mathbf{A}$ ~ $\mathbf{E}$ refer to the complete chemical formulas of the species, and these species can exist with strong stability under normal temperature and pressure.

How many of the following descriptions are correct?

- The most common crystal form of $\mathbf{A}$ is cubic crystal system
- The molecular weight of $\mathbf{E}$ is greater than 400
- The cation of $\mathbf{B}$ is composed of multiple atoms
- $\mathbf{D}$ has poor water solubility
- The yellow color of $\mathbf{A}$ dissolving in water is due to the ionization of a Brønsted acid
- The molecular weight of $\mathbf{C}$ rounded down is a prime number

For the following two polypeptide fragments ($\rm{P1/P2}$) in a protein:

<MultiModal>![Fragment 1 (P1) SMARTS: [*]-[N:2]-[C@@:1]([C:28]([C:29])[C:30])-[C:3](=[O:4])-[N:5]-[C@@:6]([C@@:7]([C:8])[C:9]-[C:10])-[C:11](=[O:12])-[N:13]-[C@@:14]([C@:15]([O:16])[C:17])-[C:18](=[O:19])-[N:20]-[C@@:21]([C:22]([C:23])[C:24])-[C:25](=[O:26])-[N:27]-[*]](figures/superchem_bdba5ec3-0c27-48a7-99ea-2b7606eeb439__1.png)</MultiModal>

<MultiModal>![Fragment 2 (P2) SMARTS: [*]-[N:3]-[C@@:2]([C:1]-[c:33]1[c:34][c:35][c:36]([O:39])[c:37][c:38]1)-[C:4](=[O:5])-[N:6]-[C@@:7]([C:10]([C:8])[C:9])-[C:11](=[O:12])-[N:13]-[C@@:14]([C:15]-[C:16]([C:17])[C:18])-[C:19](=[O:20])-[N:21]-[C@@:22]([C:23]-[c:24]1[c:28][c:29][c:30][c:31][c:32]1)-[C:25](=[O:26])-[N:27]-[*]](figures/superchem_bdba5ec3-0c27-48a7-99ea-2b7606eeb439__2.png)</MultiModal>

The two polypeptide fragments in the protein can undergo parallel $\beta$-sheet and antiparallel $\beta$-sheet formation. It is known that in each possible folding pairing mode, only the inter-amide hydrogen bond pairing links between the fragments are considered, and the hydrogen bond links with amino acid residues outside the fragments are not considered. At the same time, the number of hydrogen bonds formed between the two polypeptide fragments is the same in each folding pairing mode.

In each of the two polypeptide fragments paired by $\beta$-sheet, define:

$$S_1 = \sum_ia_{1,i}-\sum_jh_{1,j}$$

$$S_2 = \sum_ia_{2,i}-\sum_jh_{2,j}$$

where the subscript $_{1,2}$ is used to distinguish the two polypeptide fragments, $a_{1,i}$ represents the atomic number of the hydrogen bond acceptor in polypeptide fragment $1$, $h_{1,i}$ represents the atomic number of the hydrogen bond donor in polypeptide fragment $1$, $a_{2,i}$ represents the atomic number of the hydrogen bond acceptor in polypeptide fragment $2$, and $h_{2,i}$ represents the atomic number of the hydrogen bond donor in polypeptide fragment $2$.

Further define the parameter $z_n$, the value of which is calculated as follows:

$$
z_n = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{S_1 \cdot S_2}{\left(\min\{S_1, S_2\}\right)^2}\quad\quad \text{if parallel }\beta\text{-sheet}\\
\dfrac{S_1 \cdot S_2}{\left(\max\{S_1, S_2\}\right)^2}\quad\quad \text{if antiparallel }\beta\text{-sheet}\\
\end{cases}
$$

The subscript $_{n}$ represents different $\beta$-sheet pairing combinations forming different hydrogen bonds, and its value is $1,2,\cdots$.

Please observe the two polypeptide fragments and calculate the value of $\max{(z_n)},\,n=1,2,\cdots$.

stem:
The determination of glucose content in a protein sample is usually performed using spectrophotometry. Weigh $12.2 \mathrm{~g}$ of the sample, dissolve it in water, add saturated sodium chloride solution, filter, and dilute to $250 \mathrm{~mL}$ to obtain the test solution $X$. Prepare glucose standard solutions of different concentrations, take $5.00 \mathrm{~mL}$ of each solution, add $4.00 \mathrm{~mL}$ of Fehling's reagent, dilute to $10 \mathrm{~mL}$ with water, heat in a boiling water bath for 30 minutes, centrifuge, take the supernatant, and measure its absorbance at $660 \mathrm{~nm}$. Treat the test solution $X$ in the same way. The experimental data obtained are shown in the following table:

| Concentration $c(\mathrm{~g} \cdot \mathrm{L}^{-1})$ | Absorbance $A$ |
|----------|--------|
| 0.150    | 0.660  |
| 0.250    | 0.568  |
| 0.350    | 0.466  |
| 0.450    | 0.383  |
| 0.550    | 0.284  |
| 0.650    | 0.188  |
|      $X$    | 0.348  |

In addition to spectrophotometry, we can also use titration to determine the glucose content. Pipette $10.00 \mathrm{~mL}$ of Fehling's reagent, add $10 \mathrm{~mL}$ of water and $5 \mathrm{~mL}$ of potassium ferrocyanide solution, add two glass beads, heat quickly to boiling, and use methylene blue as an indicator. Titrate rapidly with a $0.500 \mathrm{~g} \cdot \mathrm{L}^{-1}$ glucose standard solution until the solution becomes colorless, consuming a volume of $15.00 \mathrm{~mL}$. Titrate with the test solution $X$ as the titrant using the same method, consuming a volume of $15.80 \mathrm{~mL}$.

Please combine the aforementioned analysis process, analyze the role of each step, and select the matching options.

Organic extractant $\mathrm{H}\bf{A}$ can extract $\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}$ from aqueous solution into the organic phase in the form of $\mathrm{Ce}(\bf{A})_x(\mathrm{H}\bf{A})_y$. $\mathrm{H}\bf{A}$ is almost insoluble in water, but exists in the organic phase only as a dimer of $\mathrm{{H_2}\bf{A}\mathrm{_2}}$. In order to determine the specific form of this cerium complex in the organic phase, the following experiment was carried out: A tracer amount of $^{144}\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}$ was dissolved in water and acidified with a small amount of nitric acid to prepare an aqueous phase containing $^{144}\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}$; $\mathrm{2.50~mL}$ each of the above aqueous phase and the organic phase containing $\mathrm{H}\bf{A}$ were transferred and thoroughly mixed and extracted at room temperature. After equilibrium, $\mathrm{1.00~mL}$ each of the aqueous phase and the organic phase were taken, and the ratio of their radioactivity intensities was measured; another portion of the equilibrated aqueous phase was taken to measure its $\mathrm{pH}$ value. When the initial concentration of $\mathrm{{H_2}\bf{A}\mathrm{_2}}$ is $c_{0}(\mathrm{{H_2}\bf{A}\mathrm{_2}}) = 0.240~\mathrm{mol/L}$, the ratio of the radioactivity intensities of the organic phase to the aqueous phase at equilibrium is measured to be $\mathrm2929:416$, and the aqueous phase $\mathrm{[H^+]} = 3.39 \times 10^{-2}~\mathrm{mol/L}$; when $c_{0}(\mathrm{{H_2}\bf{A}\mathrm{_2}}) = 0.120~\mathrm{mol/L}$, the ratio of the radioactivity intensities of the organic phase to the aqueous phase at equilibrium is measured to be $\mathrm1542:1682$, and the aqueous phase $\mathrm{[H^+]} = 3.42 \times 10^{-2}~\mathrm{mol/L}$.
The following statements are made:

1. The sum of $x$ and $y$ is an even number (treat $x$ and $y$ as integers).
2. The sum of the coefficients on both sides of the simplified and balanced extraction reaction equation are not equal.
3. The equilibrium constant of the extraction reaction is smaller than $\mathrm0.023$.
4. The equilibrium constant of the extraction reaction is smaller than $\mathrm0.015$.
5. The equilibrium constant should be taken to $\mathrm2$ significant figures.

The hydrolysis of $\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}$ and the complexation of $\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}$ with $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ are not considered in the calculation of the equilibrium constant. What is the sum of the correct serial numbers?

Organic extractant $\mathrm{H}\bf{A}$ can extract $\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}$ from aqueous solution into the organic phase in the form of $\mathrm{Ce}(\bf{A})_x(\mathrm{H}\bf{A})_y$. $\mathrm{H}\bf{A}$ is almost insoluble in water, but exists in the organic phase only as a dimer of $\mathrm{{H_2}\bf{A}\mathrm{_2}}$. In order to determine the specific form of this cerium complex in the organic phase, the following experiment was carried out: A tracer amount of $^{144}\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}$ was dissolved in water and acidified with a small amount of nitric acid to prepare an aqueous phase containing $^{144}\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}$; $\mathrm{2.50~mL}$ each of the above aqueous phase and the organic phase containing $\mathrm{H}\bf{A}$ were transferred and thoroughly mixed and extracted at room temperature. After equilibrium, $\mathrm{1.00~mL}$ each of the aqueous phase and the organic phase were taken, and the ratio of their radioactivity intensities was measured; another portion of the equilibrated aqueous phase was taken to measure its $\mathrm{pH}$ value. When the initial concentration of $\mathrm{{H_2}\bf{A}\mathrm{_2}}$ is $c_{0}(\mathrm{{H_2}\bf{A}\mathrm{_2}}) = 0.240~\mathrm{mol/L}$, the ratio of the radioactivity intensities of the organic phase to the aqueous phase at equilibrium is measured to be $\mathrm2929:416$, and the aqueous phase $\mathrm{[H^+]} = 3.39 \times 10^{-2}~\mathrm{mol/L}$; when $c_{0}(\mathrm{{H_2}\bf{A}\mathrm{_2}}) = 0.120~\mathrm{mol/L}$, the ratio of the radioactivity intensities of the organic phase to the aqueous phase at equilibrium is measured to be $\mathrm1542:1682$, and the aqueous phase $\mathrm{[H^+]} = 3.42 \times 10^{-2}~\mathrm{mol/L}$.
The following statements are made:

1. The sum of $x$ and $y$ is an even number (treat $x$ and $y$ as integers).
2. The sum of the coefficients on both sides of the simplified and balanced extraction reaction equation are not equal.
3. The equilibrium constant of the extraction reaction is smaller than $\mathrm0.023$.
4. The equilibrium constant of the extraction reaction is smaller than $\mathrm0.015$.
5. The equilibrium constant should be taken to $\mathrm2$ significant figures.

The hydrolysis of $\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}$ and the complexation of $\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}$ with $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ are not considered in the calculation of the equilibrium constant. What is the sum of the correct serial numbers?

It has been discovered that alkali metal oxides can induce the disproportionation reaction of gold. Dissolving $\mathrm{Rb_2O}$ in molten rubidium metal, adding gold metal, and heating to $200^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for 14 days yields an orthorhombic crystal. The structure of this crystal is shown below and can be viewed as a stacking of two types of layers, A and B. In the diagram, all cube vertices represent a rubidium atom, each hollow cube center contains a rubidium atom, while each white and black cube center contains a gold atom; oxygen atoms are located at the interfaces between all white cubes and hollow cubes. The structure is as follows:

<MultiModal>![On the left is a stacking structure composed of hollow cube frameworks, black cubes, and white cubes, and on the right is its layered decomposition, with a black arrow pointing from the right to the left. In the left stacking structure, the left-right direction aligns with the cube edges, while the up-down and front-back directions align with the cube face diagonals. In the right decomposed structure, from top to bottom, it splits into five layers: A, B, A, B, A. Layer A consists of hollow cube frameworks and white cubes, with the front-back direction showing the same type of cubes sharing edges and the left-right direction showing different types of cubes sharing faces. Adjacent A layers are staggered left-right for the same type of cubes. Layer B consists solely of black cubes, with the front-back direction forming a zigzag structure through face-sharing and the left-right direction also face-sharing. In the left stacking structure, adjacent black cube layers are connected via shared edges, while adjacent white-hollow cube layers have no direct connection.](figures/superchem_c41ac11f-fad1-48b2-a309-b4fd6b09f01f__1.png)</MultiModal>

Calculate the variance of the oxidation states of gold in this crystal.

stem:
Proteins possess a rich hierarchical structure, and it is this complex and subtle structure that endows proteins with many functions, such as catalysis, transport, and information transfer, making them widely and importantly applied in fields such as biochemistry and medicine. For chemists, the ability to artificially synthesize protein analogs would expand the structural range of biological macromolecules and allow for more precise control in protein modification and other aspects. In 2021, Marcus Weck's group synthesized polyisocyanides that can mimic the secondary and tertiary structures of proteins, and the related results were published on MRC. Note: PMDETA is pentamethyldiethylenetriamine, and the terminal group structure of $\bf{C}$ does not need to be explicitly defined.

<MultiModal>![Reaction of styrene with `CC(Br)C1=CC=CC=C1` in the presence of cuprous bromide and PMDETA at 100°C to obtain $\bf{A}$, $\bf{A}$ first reacts with sodium azide in DMF at room temperature, and then reacts with lithium aluminum hydride in THF to obtain $\bf{B}$, $\bf{B}$ reacts with `C[C@@H](C(=O)NCC(=O)OCC1=C(C(=C(C(=C1F)F)F)F)F)[N+]#[C-]` in DCM in the presence of $[Ni(CN^tBu)_4][ClO_4]_2$ to obtain $\bf{C}$](figures/superchem_c4c77bbb-3b2e-414e-b6af-c8eb446685dd__1.png)</MultiModal>

The following statements are made:

1. Each molecule of $\bf{B}$ contains 1 $sp^3$ nitrogen atom.

2. $\bf{B}$ contains independent methyl groups and the carbon atom connected to the methyl group is bonded to a heteroatom.

3. A certain segment of $\bf{C}$ can coil into a β-helix-like structure, and the helical structure formed by this segment has a high inversion energy barrier and will not unwind even in strongly polar protic solvents. This segment is a polyisocyanide block.

4. Two segments of $\bf{C}$ have further folded. However, if the monomer added in the step from $\bf{B}$ to $\bf{C}$ is replaced with the following compound, folding will not occur. The main intermolecular force causing this folding is π-π stacking.

<MultiModal>![[C-]#[N+][C@@H](C)C(NCCCCCC(OCC1=CC=CC=C1)=O)=O](figures/superchem_c4c77bbb-3b2e-414e-b6af-c8eb446685dd__2.png)</MultiModal>

Then the sum of the coefficients of all correct statements is:

The basic process of crude salt purification is as follows:

Dissolve $10~g$ of crude salt in $40~mL$ of deionized water with heating, then add $\mathrm{25\%~BaCl_2}$ solution to it until no more precipitate is produced, keep warm for $10~min$, and perform the first normal pressure filtration. Then add saturated $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ solution until no more precipitate is produced, and perform the second normal pressure filtration. Add 6 M hydrochloric acid, then evaporate by heating in a water bath, filter under suction to remove the mother liquor, and finally dry by stir-frying to obtain refined salt.

Assume that $10~g$ of crude salt is composed of $9~g$ $\mathrm{NaCl}$, $0.3~g$ $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$, $0.3~g$ $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $0.2~g$ $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ and $0.2~g$ $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$. It is known that $\mathrm{BaCl_2}$ and $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ are added with a 50% excess, $1~mL$ of solution is lost in each normal pressure filtration, and $5~mL$ of mother liquor is lost in vacuum filtration. Estimate the theoretical yield and theoretical yield rate based on the following solubility data.

Hint: It is considered that the volume of the solution remains unchanged and remains at $40~mL$ before evaporation and concentration, that is, deionized water will be added after the volume decreases (such as after normal pressure filtration), and the excess water will evaporate after the volume increases; vacuum filtration is performed immediately after evaporation and concentration, and it can be considered that the temperature at this time is about the boiling point of water; it is considered that $1~mL$ of aqueous solution contains $1~mL$ of water.

The data in the table below is the mass fraction of solute in saturated $\mathrm{NaCl}$ solution.

|Temperature|Mass Fraction|
|---|---|
|$25\degree C$|26.45%|
|$100\degree C$|28.05%|

In liquid ammonia at $\mathrm{238\ K}$, sodium and white phosphorus react at a certain molar ratio to form a yellow crystal. Further analysis indicates that this yellow crystal is a $1:1$ ionic compound; both its cation and anion are mononuclear sodium coordination ions, each with a coordination number of $5$. The molar mass of this ligand is $\mathrm{96\ g/mol}$, and all phosphorus atoms satisfy the octet rule.

The element **X** exhibits stable properties with strong corrosion resistance, capable of withstanding corrosion from hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, nitric acid, and aqua regia at room temperature. Fusing the elemental **X** with potassium nitrate and potassium hydroxide yields **A**. After cooling the melt, it is extracted with water and treated with chlorine gas, followed by heating to volatilize **B**. Introducing **B** into a hydrochloric acid solution and heating it, then adding ammonium chloride precipitates element **X** in the form of **C**, which, upon ignition in hydrogen gas, yields spongy elemental **X**. In a hydrochloric acid solution of potassium chloride, reducing **B** with ethanol produces the red crystalline compound **D**, in which the mass fraction of **X** is $26.99\%$. Heating **D** to $200 ℃$ results in a weight loss of $4.81\%$, yielding the brown crystalline compound **E**. If **B** is replaced with **A** as the reactant, a deep-red diamagnetic dinuclear complex **F** is obtained, in which the mass fraction of **X** is $27.73\%$. Dissolving **F** in concentrated hydrochloric acid and adding ammonia water generates a 1:3 ionic compound **G**. Exposing the solution of **G** to air produces a vivid red color, from which the diamagnetic compound **H** can be isolated. **H** is named for its intense color. Oxidizing **H** with ammonium cerium(IV) sulfate yields the paramagnetic brown compound **I**. It is known that both **H** and **I** are trinuclear complexes with identical cationic chemical formulas, where the mass fraction of **X** in the cation is $52.86\%$, while the anion count ratio is 6:7.  

Given that **A**~**I** are all compounds containing **X**, which of the following options are correct?

Trace element $\mathbf{X}$ is named after a Western European country. Extraction of $\mathbf{X}$ from minerals of elements from the same group requires a complex process, in which the key step is the formation of a precipitate $\mathbf{A}$ containing $\mathbf{X}$ and a precipitate $\mathbf{B}$ of the same type but without $\mathbf{Χ}$ to enrich $\mathbf{X}$.

The element $\mathbf{X}$ can react with a colorless irritating gas $\mathbf{C}$ to form a gray semi-metallic solid $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{D}$-type compounds have important industrial applications.

A monovalent anion $\mathbf{E}$ containing a mass fraction of $37.11\%$ of $\mathbf{X}$ has a $C_2$ axis and 4 bridging bonds, while the neutral compound $\mathbf{F}$ with the same elemental composition as $\mathbf{E}$ exhibits a $+2$ apparent valence for $\mathbf{X}$, but in reality, there is an anion-cation pair. $\mathbf{F}$ dissolves in diethyl ether to obtain a solvate $\mathbf{G}$, which also contains discrete anions and cations with the same coordination number for the anions and cations.

The reaction of $LiBH_4$ with a high-valent halide of $\mathbf{X}$ at $-45\degree C$ yields a ternary compound $\mathbf{H}$, where $\omega_\mathbf{X}=69.43\%$, which can be approximately considered to have $C_{2v}$ symmetry.

A binary compound $\mathbf{I}$ of $\mathbf{X}$ can be prepared below $308K$. Its monomer is a viscous liquid with slight polarity, while the polymer is a white solid. Both have strong reducing properties. The $1:1$ adduct formed by $\mathbf{I}$ with ligand $\mathbf{J}$ can be used to prepare $\mathbf{I}$ and can also form a $1:2$ complex $\mathbf{K}$, whose configuration is different from $\mathbf{H}$.

$\mathbf{C, J, D}$ contain the same element, and $\mathbf{J}$ can be prepared by complete methylation of $\mathbf{C}$.

Given the following options for the above process, let $x$ be the product of the serial numbers of all incorrect statements, and $y$ be the sum of the serial numbers of all correct statements. Find $\dfrac{\sqrt x}{y+1}$ and select the option with an absolute error $<0.001$, if there is no option that meets the condition, choose $A$.

2. Gas $\mathbf{C}$ dissolves in water to give an acidic solution

4. One $C_2$ axis of anion $\mathbf{E}$ passes through a hexacoordinate atom and two ligands

8. Compound $\mathbf{I}$ is extremely prone to decompose into its elemental form at room temperature

9. The number of atoms of each element in ligand $\mathbf{J}$ constitutes a geometric sequence

10. The configuration of complex $\mathbf{K}$ is square pyramidal

The following reactions control the stepwise hydrolysis and sulfur substitution sequence of molybdate and thiomolybdate in dilute aqueous solution (the concentration of water is already included in the equilibrium constant):

$\mathrm{MoS_4^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{MoOS_3^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2S(aq.)} \quad K_1 = 1.3 \times 10^{-5}$

$\mathrm{MoOS_3^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{MoO_2S_2^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2S(aq.)} \quad K_2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$

$\mathrm{MoO_2S_2^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{MoO_3S^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2S(aq.)} \quad K_3 = 1.6 \times 10^{-5}$

$\mathrm{MoO_3S^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{MoO_4^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2S(aq.)} \quad K_4 = 6.5 \times 10^{-6}$

$\mathrm{MoS_4^{2-}}$ with an initial concentration of $2.00\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{mol\;L^{-1}}$ undergoes hydrolysis in a buffer solution at $\text{pH}=5.00$. Considering the ionization and volatilization of $\mathrm{H_2S(aq.)}$, it is known that:

- The buffer capacity is large enough that the $\text{pH}$ does not change, and the buffer species do not interfere with the given reactions.
- $\mathrm{p}K_{a1} = 6.88,\; \mathrm{p}K_{a2} = 12.90$ for $\mathrm{H_2S}$
- The solution volume is $V_{\rm aq}=1.00\ \mathrm{L}$, and the gas phase volume above is $V_{\rm g}=5.00\ \mathrm{L}$ (the whole system is closed)
- Henry's constant for $\mathrm{H_2S}$ is $H = 9.741\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{atm}/(\mathrm{mol}\cdot\mathrm{m^{-3}})$
- Take $T=298.15\ \mathrm{K}$, and the ideal gas constant is $R=0.082057\ \mathrm{L\;atm\;mol^{-1}\;K^{-1}}$

The final result should retain the appropriate number of significant figures, and choose the option within $10\%$ of the calculated result; otherwise, choose option A: All other options are incorrect.

The element $\mathbf M$ of the first transition series dissolves in dilute sulfuric acid and crystallizes to obtain a hydrated sulfate crystal $\mathbf A$, in which the mass fraction of $\mathbf M$ is 20.97%. Element $\mathbf M$ has only one non-radioactive stable isotope.

The THF solvate of the simple chloride of $\mathbf M$ reacts with 1-lithiated bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane in pentane to produce $\mathbf M$ element and a mononuclear, electrically neutral complex $\mathbf D$ with a carbon content of 76.50%.

Reduction of $\mathbf D$ with lithium element in tetrahydrofuran yields a salt $\mathbf E$ with a cation-anion ratio of 1:1, while oxidation of $\mathbf D$ with silver tetrafluoroborate yields a salt $\mathbf F$ with a cation-anion ratio of 1:1.

Regarding the above content, there are the following conclusions:

Conclusion 1: Isotope $\mathbf M_2$ whose mass number is 1 greater than that of the stable isotope of $\mathbf M$ emits β rays when decaying.

Conclusion 2: The molecular weight of $\mathbf D$ is 583.77.

Conclusion 3: $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf E$, and $\mathbf F$ all contain $\mathbf M$ with an octahedral coordination configuration.

Conclusion 4: The theoretically calculated spin-only magnetic moment of $\mathbf E$ is 2.83 B.M..

Conclusion 5: $\mathbf F$ is a diamagnetic substance.

Select the option corresponding to all the correct conclusions.

stem:
Due to the unique properties of metal-metal bonds, the synthesis of metal string complexes has consistently garnered widespread attention from researchers. A common method for synthesizing the ligand $\bf A$ for metal strings is as follows: Under an argon atmosphere, substrate $\bf B$ (1.98 g, 23 mmol) and $\bf C$ (2.16 g, 10 mmol), $\rm t-BuOK$ (2.81 g, 25 mmol), $\rm Pd_2(dba)_3$ (183 mg, 0.20 mmol), $\rm dppp$ (165 mg, 0.40 mmol) were added to a dry flask. The mixture was stirred and refluxed in toluene (100 mL) for 48 hours, and the system was observed to turn dark brown. The solvent was removed under reduced pressure, and then the mixture was poured into water. The precipitate was filtered to obtain a solid, which was purified by silica gel column chromatography using ethyl acetate as the eluent to obtain a bright yellow product $\bf A$. It is known that dppp is a bidentate phosphine ligand, and the structures of $\bf B$ and $\bf C$ are as follows:

<MultiModal>![The SMILES of $\bf B$ is NC1=NC=CC=C1, and the SMILES of $\bf C$ is ClC1=NC2=C(C=C1)C=CC(Cl)=N2](figures/superchem_cd253406-ce46-4edb-95f4-9165fcae0393__1.png)</MultiModal>

A mixture of $\bf A$ (251 mg), naphthalene (25 g), and $\rm DMF$ (5 mL) was placed in a conical flask and heated to 100 $\rm\degree C$. Then $\rm t-BuOK$ (224 mg, 2.0 mmol) was slowly added, and the system immediately turned dark brown. It was heated at approximately 130~140 $\rm\degree C$ for 15 hours, and then refluxed at 200 ℃ for 15 minutes to obtain an orange transparent solution. Anhydrous $\rm CoCl_2$ (182 mg, 1.4 mmol) was added dropwise, and after refluxing for another 30 minutes, $\rm NaSCN$ (32 mg, 0.40 mmol) was slowly added, and the color changed from dark brown to dark green. The mixture was refluxed for another 3 hours, then concentrated to approximately 5 mL, and then cooled to 70 ℃. It was treated with hexane, and the metal complex precipitated. The precipitate was collected by suction filtration and washed with hexane to remove naphthalene and $\rm DMF$. The solid was extracted with $\rm CH_2Cl_2$ and filtered. The $\rm CH_2Cl_2$ solution was treated with excess $\rm KPF_6$ in methanol and stirred overnight, and then the solvent was removed under vacuum. The remaining solid was extracted with $\rm CH_2Cl_2$ and filtered. Pentane vapor was slowly diffused into the filtrate to obtain dark purple 1:1 salt $\bf D$. The mass fractions of each element in $\bf D$ (all theoretical values) are as follows: $\rm Co$ 18.14%, $\rm C$ 46.22%, $\rm H$ 2.59%, $\rm N$ 18.69%. It is known that all coordinating atoms in the complex are the same.

$\bf D$ was treated with $\rm [Cp_2Fe](PF_6)$ in $\rm CH_2Cl_2/MeOH$ in a 1:1 reaction to obtain $\bf E$.

At room temperature, the highest occupied single electron of $\bf D$ occupies $\delta ^*(6)$; the highest occupied two single electrons of $\bf E$ occupy $\delta ^*(6)$ and $\sigma ^*(4)$ with similar energy levels, respectively.

Which of the following statements are correct:
1.  Given that the average bond order of the $\rm Co-Co$ bond in $\bf D$ is 0.5, then $\rm Co$ all satisfy the 18-electron rule.
2.  There are 38 atoms involved in coordination in all anions and cations of $\bf E$, and there are 2 types of coordinating atoms.
3.  In the process of preparing $\bf D$, a substance must have been oxidized in the reaction system.
4.  Considering the distance between the farthest $\rm Co$ atoms, $\bf D$>$\bf E$
5.  The magnetic moments of $\bf D$ and $\bf E$ vary with temperature as shown in the figure below:
<MultiModal>![This image is a two-dimensional scatter plot with lines against a white background. The vertical Y-axis is labeled "$\rm μ_{eff}$ (B.M.)", with a scale starting from 0 and incrementing upwards to 1, 2, and 3. The horizontal X-axis is labeled "$\rm T$ (K)", with a scale starting from 0 and incrementing to the right with values 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, and 300. The plot shows two curves formed by discrete data points, as indicated in the legend: black squares represent compound $\bf 1$, and white circles represent compound $\bf 2$. The first curve, represented by solid black squares, has a $\rm μ_{eff}$ value of approximately 1.9 in the very low temperature region near 0 K, which then remains essentially constant, forming a flat region up to about T = 75 K. After 75 K, the $\rm μ_eff$ value of this curve increases very slowly with increasing temperature, reaching about 2.1 at 300 K. The second curve, represented by hollow white circles, has a $\rm μ_{eff}$ value below 1.0, around 0.8, near 0 K. As the temperature T increases, the $\rm μ_{eff}$ value of this curve continues to rise significantly, with a higher rate of increase in the low-temperature region, which gradually slows down as the temperature increases. At approximately T = 80 K, this hollow circle curve intersects with the solid square curve, where the $\rm μ_{eff}$ value is slightly below 2.0. At T = 300 K, the hollow circle curve reaches its highest point in the graph, with a $\rm μ_{eff}$ value of approximately 2.8.](figures/superchem_cd253406-ce46-4edb-95f4-9165fcae0393__2.png)</MultiModal>

Then the black squares represent $\bf E$, and the white circles represent $\bf D$

Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) is a classical thermodynamic method for determining biomolecular interactions, renowned as the "gold standard" for biomolecular interaction studies due to its high sensitivity and accuracy. Da Congming discovered in experiments that two chemically synthesized small molecules, $A$ and $B$, can inhibit the function of enzyme $E$. Anxious, he planned to directly use ITC to measure and compare the binding abilities of the two molecules to the enzyme, conducting the following experiments:

1.  Titration of $15$ ${\mu} M$ protein $E$ directly with $250$ ${\mu}M A$. The fitting results yielded a stoichiometry ratio of $n=1$, $ΔH =-7.6$ $kcal · mol ^{-1}$, but failed to fit $K_d$.
2.  Titration of $15$ ${\mu} M$ protein $E$ directly with $250$ ${\mu} B$. The fitting results yielded $n=1$, $ΔH = 7.3$ $kcal · mol ^{-1}$, $K_d = 0.41$ ${\mu}M$.
3.  Mixing a 10-fold excess of $B$ with $15$ ${\mu} M$ $E$, and then titrating with $250$ ${\mu} M$ $A$. Under these conditions, the measured values were $n=0.87$, $ΔH = -4.8$ $kcal · mol ^{-1}$, $K_d = 15.5$ $nM$.

Based on the above information, which of the following options is most likely the binding constant $K_a$ of $A$ and $E$?

The following operations were performed on the powdered metal $\mathbf{M}$:

1. Step 1: After heating, the powder slowly dissolves in concentrated sulfuric acid, producing a gas $\mathbf{A}$ with a pungent odor.  
2. Step 2: A small amount of the solution is mixed with pyridine, and hydrogen peroxide solution is slowly added under low-temperature conditions. The solution turns blue, forming a mononuclear pentagonal pyramidal complex $\mathbf{B}$. If pyridine is replaced with bipyridine, the product undergoes only minor changes.  
3. Step 3: KOH solution is added to the sulfuric acid solution of $\mathbf{M}$ until nearly neutral, resulting in a gray-green precipitate $\mathbf{C}$.  
4. Step 4: Continued addition of KOH solution dissolves the precipitate, forming a colored ion $\mathbf{D}$ in the solution.  
5. Step 5: Hydrogen peroxide is added to the solution, causing a color change. Cooling and crystallization yield a solid $\mathbf{E}$.  
6. Step 6: An appropriate amount of solid $\mathbf{E}$ is dissolved in a relatively concentrated sulfuric acid solution, producing a red solution containing two ions $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$, both of which appear red. $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ are trinuclear and tetranuclear oxoacid ions, respectively, each carrying a double negative charge.  

Please select the correct option.

The laboratory uses the following method to determine the content of mercury sulfide $(HgS)$ in cinnabar samples:

(1) Weigh $3.2643 g$ of dried primary standard sodium chloride, dissolve it in water, and dilute to a $500.0 mL$ volumetric flask.

(2) Transfer $25.00mL$ of sodium chloride solution, add $50.00mL$ of silver nitrate solution, $5mL$ of nitric acid, and 10 drops of indicator $\mathbf{A}$, and titrate with $NH_4SCN$ solution to the endpoint, consuming $23.97mL$.

(3) Transfer $25.00mL$ of silver nitrate solution, add $5mL$ of nitric acid, and 10 drops of indicator $\mathbf{A}$, and titrate with $NH_4SCN$ solution to the endpoint, consuming $26.26mL$.

(4) Weigh another $0.2846g$ of the cinnabar sample into another test tube, add $10mL$ of sulfuric acid and $1.5g$ of potassium nitrate, and heat to dissolve, producing a reddish-brown gas and a pale yellow precipitate; after cooling, add $10g\cdot L^{-1}$ potassium permanganate solution dropwise until pink, the precipitate disappears, and then boil the solution until colorless, and no precipitate is formed in this step.

(5) Add ten drops of indicator $\mathbf{A}$, and titrate with the above ammonium thiocyanate solution to the endpoint, consuming $22.83mL$.

Regarding the above experimental process, there are the following statements:

(1) The concentration of the $NaCl$ solution is $0.112mol\cdot L^{-1}$

(2) The concentration of the $NH_4SCN$ solution is $0.1182mol\cdot L^{-1}$

(3) The concentration of the $AgNO_3$ solution is $0.1125mol\cdot L^{-1}$

(4) In the chemical reaction equation for dissolving the cinnabar sample, if the equation is balanced according to the simplest reaction ratio, the reaction coefficient of $H_2SO_4$ is 3

(5) When adding potassium permanganate solution dropwise, if the ion equation is balanced according to the simplest reaction ratio, the coefficient of $H_2O$ in the equation is 4

(6) $\mathbf{A}$ in the question can be ferric chloride

(7) The content of mercury sulfide in the cinnabar sample is $91.27\%$

Among the above statements, the number of correct ones is (pay attention to significant figures, if the number of significant figures is too small, it should be treated as incorrect; for options involving calculations, if the error is less than $1\%$, it is considered correct)

1. The triple point of water is $273.16 \mathrm{~K}$, and the freezing point is $273.15 \mathrm{~K}$.
2. The relationship between the freezing point and pressure is $\Delta \mathrm{T} / \Delta \mathrm{P}=-7.432 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~K} / \mathrm{Pa}$.
3. At the triple point, the vapor pressure of water is $610.48 \mathrm{~Pa}$.
4. The volume fractions of nitrogen and oxygen in the air are $79 \%$ and $21 \%$, and their Henry's constants are $1.035 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~mol} \cdot \mathrm{L}^{-1} / \mathrm{kPa}$ and $2.154 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~mol} \cdot \mathrm{L}^{-1}/ \mathrm{kPa}$, respectively.
5. The atmospheric pressure is $101325 \mathrm{~Pa}$, and the acceleration due to gravity is taken as $9.8 ~m/s^2$.

Based on the known information, the problems to be calculated are:

stem:
Salt $\mathbf{A}$ contains the metallic element $\mathbf{Z}$ with a mass fraction of 57.77%. When heated to $400^\circ C$, salt $\mathbf{A}$ decomposes with a weight loss of 11.144%, releasing the elemental gas $\mathbf{X}$. The solid elemental substance $\mathbf{Y}$ can react with gas $\mathbf{X}$ in different proportions to form two binary compounds, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$. $\mathbf{B}$ is a liquid with a mass ratio of 1.336 between its two elements, while $\mathbf{C}$ is a gas with a density approximately 9 times that of air under STP conditions.  

$\mathbf{A}$ can dissolve in $\mathbf{B}$ to form a solution (denoted as Solution 1). When gas $\mathbf{D}$ is passed into Solution 1 (Reaction 1), $\mathbf{D}$ is oxidized to the cation $\mathbf{D}^+$, and the elemental form of $\mathbf{Z}$ precipitates. The remaining part, after vacuum distillation, yields salt $\mathbf{E}$, which shares the same cation $\mathbf{D}^+$ as $\mathbf{A}$.  

If $\mathbf{F}$ is added to Solution 1 instead, $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{F}$ react in a 1:1:1 ratio to form the ionic compound $\mathbf{G}$ (Reaction 2). The structure of $\mathbf{G}$ is distinctive, as both its cation and anion belong to the $O_{h}$ point group and are isoelectronic with each other.  

Salt $\mathbf{H}$ has the same anion as $\mathbf{A}$, but its molar mass is 2 g/mol greater than that of $\mathbf{A}$. When $\mathbf{H}$ reacts with $\mathbf{B}$, it releases the colorless gas $\mathbf{W}$ (Reaction 3). At room temperature, $\mathbf{W}$ can combine with $\mathbf{D}$ to form a reddish-brown gas, which can further dimerize.  

The above transformations can be represented by the following reaction equations:  

1. $\mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{400^\circ C} \cdots \mathbf{X}$  

2. $\mathbf{X} \xrightarrow{\mathbf{Y}} \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{C}$  

3. $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathbf{D}]{\text{Rxn 1}} \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{Z}$  

4. $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B} \xrightarrow[\mathbf{F}]{\text{Rxn 2}} \mathbf{G}$  

5. $\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{H} \xrightarrow{\text{Rxn 3}} \mathbf{W}$  

6. $\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{D} \rightarrow \text{brown gas}$  

Based on the above information, select the most appropriate option from the following choices.

Sodium azide is a commonly used reagent in organic chemistry. In the laboratory, the purity of sodium azide is often determined by titration analysis, and the specific steps are as follows:  

1. Accurately weigh $0.4620 \mathrm{~g}$ of dried arsenic trioxide into a $250 \mathrm{~mL}$ beaker, add $100 \mathrm{~mL}$ of $100 \mathrm{~g} \cdot \mathrm{L}^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution to dissolve it, then transfer to a $1 \mathrm{~L}$ volumetric flask. Add $250 \mathrm{~mL}$ of water and $250 \mathrm{~mL}$ of $3 \mathrm{~mol} \cdot \mathrm{L}^{-1}$ sulfuric acid, and dilute to the mark.  

2. Precisely pipette $50.00 \mathrm{~mL}$ of arsenic trioxide standard solution into a $500 \mathrm{~mL}$ conical flask, add 3 drops of $2.5 \mathrm{~g} \cdot \mathrm{L}^{-1}$ osmium tetroxide solution, then add $25.00 \mathrm{~mL}$ of the ceric ammonium nitrate solution to be standardized. Dilute with water to $150 \mathrm{~mL}$, add $30 \mathrm{~mL}$ of $3 \mathrm{~mol} \cdot \mathrm{L}^{-1}$ sulfuric acid and 2 drops of ferroin indicator, and titrate with the ferrous ammonium sulfate solution to be standardized until the endpoint is reached. The titration consumes $\mathrm{39.90 ~mL}$ of ferrous ammonium sulfate standard solution.  

3. Using all the reagents mentioned above except arsenic trioxide, the titration consumes $\mathrm{49.18 ~mL}$ of ferrous ammonium sulfate standard solution.  

4. Accurately weigh $\mathrm{2.7233 ~g}$ of sodium azide sample, dissolve it in water, and dilute to $\mathrm{250 ~mL}$. Pipette $\mathrm{20.00 ~mL}$ of this solution into a $\mathrm{500 ~mL}$ conical flask, add $\mathrm{40.00 ~mL}$ of ceric ammonium nitrate standard solution, and allow the reaction to proceed in a cold water bath. After the reaction is complete, dilute to $\mathrm{150 ~mL}$, add $\mathrm{30 ~mL\ 3 ~mol\cdot L^{-1}}$ sulfuric acid and 2 drops of ferroin indicator, then titrate with ferrous ammonium sulfate standard solution until the endpoint is reached. The titration consumes $\mathrm{15.32 ~mL}$ of ferrous ammonium sulfate standard solution.  

Regarding this analytical process, the following statements are made:  

A. Dried arsenic trioxide can be directly used to prepare the standard test solution.  

B. The osmium tetroxide added undergoes a change in oxidation state during the analysis.  

C. The ionic equation for the chemical reaction occurring after adding ceric ammonium nitrate in step 2, when balanced with the simplest integer coefficients, has a sum of product coefficients equal to 5.  

D. The concentration of the prepared arsenic trioxide solution is $\mathrm{0.002335 ~mol/L}$.  

E. The concentration of the ceric ammonium nitrate solution is $\mathrm{0.09900 ~mol/L}$.  

F. The concentration of ferrous ammonium sulfate is $\mathrm{0.04032 ~mol/L}$.  

G. The content of sodium azide is $\mathrm{95.16 ~\%}$.  

Among these statements, the number of correct ones is (for calculation-related options, an error less than $\mathrm{1 ~\%}$ is considered correct).

A complex oxide $\mathrm{ABO}_{2}$ can form multiple crystal polymorphs. In the crystal structures involved in this problem, the same type of metal ions occupy identical interstitial sites, with the same coordination number and coordination polyhedra.

For the cubic phase $\alpha-\mathrm{ABO}_{2}$, X-ray diffraction measurements revealed several characteristic interplanar spacings of the crystal as 239.9, 207.7, 146.9, 125.3, and 103.9 $\mathrm{pm}$. The density of this crystal is known to be 4.389 $\mathrm{g\cdot cm^{-3}}$ with an error margin below 0.08%.

For $\gamma-\mathrm{ABO}_{2}$, the unit cell parameters were measured as $a=b=405.7 \mathrm{pm}, c=875.9 \mathrm{pm}$, with $\gamma$ unknown. This crystal can be described as: $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ alternately filling interstitial sites within layers to form polyhedral layers, where all polyhedral layers share identical chemical environments.

For another $\mathrm{ABO}_{2}$ structure, the unit cell parameters were measured as $a=b=296.3 \mathrm{pm}, c=1463.6 \mathrm{pm}$, with $\gamma$ unknown. This crystal can be viewed as having $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ arranged in alternating layers, where atoms of the same type share identical chemical environments.

Determine the identities of $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ before answering.

$\rm CuSO_4$, $\rm H_5IO_6$, $\rm K_2S_2O_8$, and $\rm KOH$ were mixed in a certain proportion, $\rm 200~mL$ of distilled water was added, heated to boiling for $\rm 30~min$, cooled, and filtered to obtain a blue-green solution (Reaction 1); an appropriate amount of $\rm 10\%~NaOH$ solution was added to it, allowed to stand for $\rm 48~h$, and blue-green crystals precipitated. Partial analysis results of the blue-green crystals are as follows:

(1) X-ray diffraction analysis showed that the crystal is a complex salt with crystal water, the cations are $\rm Na^+$ and $\rm K^+$, and the anion is a mononuclear coordination ion centered on copper, with $\rm HIO_6^{4-}$ as the ligand.

(2) $\rm 0.2001~g$ of the crystal was weighed, $\rm 10~mL$ of hydrochloric acid was added, and heated to dissolve the sample, then diluted with $\rm 50~mL$ of distilled water, buffer solution and $\rm PAN$ indicator were added, and titrated with $\rm 0.01973~mol\cdot L^{-1}~EDTA$ solution, consuming $\rm 11.81~mL$.

(3) $\rm 0.2059~g$ of the crystal was weighed, $\rm 10~mL~25\%~KI$ solution and $\rm 10~mL~25\%$ sulfuric acid solution were added (Reaction 2), after full reaction, with starch as an indicator, titrated with $\rm 0.1024~mol\cdot L^{-1}$ sodium thiosulfate solution, consuming $\rm 42.16~mL$.

(4) Thermogravimetric analysis of the crystal showed a weight loss of $\rm 25.18\%$, corresponding to the loss of all crystal water.

Which of the following statements are correct:

1.  $\rm Cu$ in the crystal is +5 valence
2.  The chemical formula of the crystal contains 12 crystal water molecules
3.  Without considering crystal water, the sum of the left and right coefficients of the chemical equation of Reaction 1 is 45
4.  Without considering crystal water, the difference between the left and right coefficients of the chemical equation of Reaction 2 is 6 (right minus left)
